subtopics.name: Aging process and older adult health

questions.stem: A nurse on a busy medical unit is planning morning care for several clients who are on standard precautions only. For each task, select every item of protective equipment the nurse should wear.

rows.text: Irrigating a draining abdominal wound where splashing is likely
Suctioning an awake client's tracheostomy with a closed system unavailable

rationale.correct: Standard precautions match PPE to expected exposure: gloves for body fluids, gowns for likely soiling and mask and eye protection for splashes or sprays.

perOption.r2:c2: Not needed unless soiling of clothing is likely.
perOption.r2:c3: Not needed unless splashing is likely.
perOption.r3:c2: Not needed unless soiling is likely.
perOption.r3:c3: Not needed unless splashing is likely.
perOption.r4:c2: A gown is used if soiling is expected.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A nurse who works in the intensive care unit arrives with new acrylic artificial nails. What should the charge nurse tell the nurse?

options.text: The nails are fine as long as the nurse wears gloves for each client contact
They are not allowed in high-risk areas because they harbor bacteria
The nails are allowed if they are shorter than 1 cm
The nails are allowed if the nurse uses extra alcohol hand rub during the shift

rationale.correct: Artificial nails and extenders harbor bacteria and are prohibited for staff caring for high-risk clients.

perOption.a: Gloves do not remove the infection risk of artificial nails.
perOption.b: Artificial nails are linked to outbreaks; CDC and most policies prohibit them for staff caring for high-risk clients.
perOption.c: Length limits apply to natural nails; artificial nails are not allowed.
perOption.d: Hand rub does not overcome the risk.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Apply hand hygiene policy on artificial nails.

questions.stem: A nursing student asks which procedures need sterile technique in the hospital. Complete the sentences.

content.template: Inserting an indwelling urinary catheter requires {{b1}} technique. Inserting a nasogastric tube requires {{b2}} technique. Changing a central venous catheter dressing requires {{b3}} technique.

options.text: sterile
clean
no special
clean
sterile
surgical scrub
sterile
clean
no special

rationale.correct: Use sterile technique for sterile body sites and central lines; clean technique for non-sterile sites such as the GI tract.

perOption.b1:a: The bladder is a sterile body cavity.
perOption.b1:b: Clean technique is not enough for a catheter into the bladder.
perOption.b2:a: The GI tract is not sterile.
perOption.b2:b: Sterile technique is not needed for the GI tract.
perOption.b2:c: A surgical scrub is not used.
perOption.b3:a: Central line dressings use sterile technique to prevent bloodstream infection.
perOption.b3:b: Clean technique is not enough for a central line.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: An infection prevention nurse observes central line care. Highlight the practices that do not follow the central line bundle.

segments.text: cleans hands and puts on sterile gloves for the dressing change
removes the old dressing and touches the insertion site with a bare finger
The site is scrubbed with chlorhexidine and allowed to dry
writes the date on a dressing that is 9 days old
The tubing connector is accessed without scrubbing the hub

rationale.correct: Central line bundle: hand hygiene, sterile dressing changes with chlorhexidine, no touching the site, timely dressing changes and hub scrubbing.

perOption.s8: Transparent dressings are changed at least every 7 days or when soiled.
perOption.s10: Hubs must be scrubbed before each access.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance

questions.stem: A nurse cared for a client for 2 days before the client was diagnosed with active pulmonary tuberculosis and placed on airborne precautions. The nurse's last tuberculin skin test a year ago was negative. What should the nurse expect?

options.text: No follow-up, since the nurse had a negative test a year ago
A test now and a repeat test 8 to 10 weeks later
Starting four-drug TB treatment right away as a precaution
A chest x-ray once a month for the next year

rationale.correct: After an unprotected TB exposure, staff are tested at baseline and 8 to 10 weeks later; positive results lead to evaluation.

perOption.a: A new exposure needs follow-up testing.
perOption.b: Exposed staff are tested soon after and again 8 to 10 weeks later, when a new infection would show.
perOption.c: Treatment is not started without evidence of infection or disease.
perOption.d: Routine monthly x-rays are not recommended.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a community group about preparing a household for disasters. Which recommendations should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keep at least a 3-day supply of water for each person
Keep a supply of prescription medications and a list of them
Keep important documents in a waterproof container
Use candles rather than flashlights during power outages
Plan a meeting place and an out-of-area contact for the family
Run a generator in the garage with the door partly open

rationale.correct: Household preparedness: water and food for several days, medications and lists, documents, flashlights, a family plan and safe generator use outdoors.

perOption.a: About 1 gallon per person per day.
perOption.f: This can cause carbon monoxide poisoning.

references: NCSBN NCLEX-RN Test Plan
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A fire starts in a client's room. Place the nurse's actions in the order of the RACE response.

items.text: Close the doors to contain the fire and smoke
Extinguish the fire if it is small, or evacuate
Remove the client from immediate danger
Activate the fire alarm and call the emergency number

rationale.correct: RACE: rescue, alarm, contain, extinguish or evacuate.
references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to a fire using RACE.

questions.stem: During a home visit to a family with a 3-year-old, which observation shows the parent needs more teaching about poisoning prevention?

options.text: Cleaning products are stored in a locked cabinet under the sink
A visitor's purse with pills in it is on the low coffee table
The poison control number is saved in the parent's phone
Medicines are kept in their original child-resistant containers on a high shelf

rationale.correct: Toddler poisoning prevention includes locked storage, original containers, poison control numbers and checking visitors' bags and purses.

perOption.b: Visitors' bags often contain medicines that toddlers can reach.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)

questions.stem: A client who is 10 weeks pregnant with a first baby works long hours, often eats prepared foods and asks about food safety. For each food, indicate whether it is safe in pregnancy or should be avoided.

rows.text: Deli turkey eaten cold from the package
Soft cheese made from unpasteurized milk
Eggs cooked until the yolk is firm

rationale.correct: In pregnancy avoid unheated deli meats, unpasteurized dairy, raw or undercooked eggs and meat and high-mercury fish; low-mercury fish is encouraged.

perOption.r1:c1: Cold deli meats can carry Listeria.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client who is breastfeeding a 3-week-old has a red, hot, tender area on one breast, a temperature of 38.6 °C (101.5 °F) and body aches. What should the nurse teach?

options.text: Stop breastfeeding on that side until the infection clears
Keep feeding or pumping often from both breasts and take the antibiotic
Switch the baby to formula until the fever is completely gone
Apply heat and cut back on fluids to reduce milk production

rationale.correct: Mastitis: keep breastfeeding or pumping from both breasts, take antibiotics as prescribed, rest, drink fluids and seek care for worsening symptoms.

perOption.a: Stopping can worsen engorgement and mastitis.
perOption.b: Frequent milk removal and antibiotics treat mastitis; the milk is safe for the baby.
perOption.c: Formula is not needed; breastfeeding helps clear the infection.
perOption.d: Fluids are needed; cold compresses after feeding often help.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A term newborn is born vaginally after a long second stage of labor. At 1 minute after birth, the newborn has a heart rate of 110/min, slow and irregular breathing, some flexion of the arms and legs, a grimace when the feet are stimulated, and a pink body with blue hands and feet. What is the newborn's Apgar score?

rationale.correct: Heart rate 110 (over 100) = 2; slow, irregular breathing = 1; some flexion = 1; grimace = 1; pink body with blue extremities = 1. Total = 6.

questions.stem: The parent of an 18-month-old says the child drinks about 1.5 L (50 oz) of whole milk a day and eats very little solid food. The child looks pale. What should the nurse recommend?

options.text: Switch to skim milk so the child is hungrier for solid foods
Limit milk to 16 to 24 oz a day and offer iron-rich foods
Add more milk to the child's diet, since milk is a good source of iron
Give milk in a bottle at bedtime to help the child sleep

rationale.correct: Toddlers should drink about 16 to 24 oz of milk a day; excess milk causes iron-deficiency anemia.

perOption.a: Toddlers need whole milk until 2 years; the amount is the problem.
perOption.b: Too much milk crowds out iron-rich foods and causes iron-deficiency anemia.
perOption.d: Bedtime bottles add to milk intake and cause tooth decay.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is planning health promotion for a 75-year-old client who lives independently. Which recommendations should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Exercise for balance and strength, such as tai chi
A yearly influenza vaccine
Regular vision and hearing checks
Stopping all physical activity to avoid injury
A review of all medications at least once a year
Routine colonoscopy every 5 years regardless of past results
Checking the home for fall hazards such as loose rugs

rationale.correct: Older adult health promotion: balance and strength exercise, vaccines, sensory checks, medication review and individualized screening.

perOption.c: Sensory problems raise fall and isolation risk.

references: U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommendations
CDC/ACIP immunization schedules

questions.stem: A 27-year-old client had a hormonal intrauterine device (IUD) placed in the clinic 3 weeks ago. Which symptom should the client be taught to report right away?

options.text: Light, irregular spotting during the first few months
Severe abdominal pain with fever and foul discharge
Lighter periods than the client had before the IUD was placed
Mild cramping for a day or two after placement

rationale.correct: IUD warning signs (PAINS): period late or abnormal bleeding, abdominal pain, infection with fever, nasty discharge and strings missing or changed.

perOption.b: These suggest pelvic infection, which needs prompt treatment.
perOption.c: Lighter periods are an expected effect of a hormonal IUD.
perOption.d: Mild cramping after placement is expected.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: For each average-risk client, choose the screening the nurse should expect to recommend.

cells.text: A 66-year-old man who smoked for 20 years
A 58-year-old with a 30 pack-year history who quit 5 years ago
A 42-year-old with breasts and no family history

options.text: Colorectal cancer screening
Lung cancer CT
Abdominal aortic aneurysm ultrasound
Abdominal aortic aneurysm ultrasound
Cervical cytology
Mammogram
Mammogram only
Annual low-dose CT of the chest
No screening
Mammogram every 2 years
Colonoscopy every year
Abdominal aortic aneurysm ultrasound

rationale.correct: Average-risk screening: colorectal from 45, mammography every 2 years from 40, AAA once for men 65 to 75 who smoked and low-dose CT for heavy smokers 50 to 80.

perOption.b2:a: One-time screen for men 65 to 75 who ever smoked.
perOption.b3:b: Recommended for ages 50 to 80 with 20 pack-years who smoke or quit within 15 years.
perOption.b3:c: Criteria for lung screening are met.

references: U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommendations
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client at 39 weeks in a first pregnancy asks when to come to the hospital. Which statement shows understanding?

options.text: "I'll come in as soon as I feel any tightening in my belly."
"I'll come in for contractions 5 minutes apart for an hour, or if my water breaks."
"I'll wait until contractions are 1 minute apart before I leave home for the hospital."
"I'll come in if the contractions stop completely for a whole day."

rationale.correct: Teach clients to come in for regular contractions (about 5-1-1), rupture of membranes, bleeding, decreased fetal movement or severe pain.

perOption.a: Irregular tightening may be Braxton Hicks contractions.
perOption.b: The 5-1-1 guide and rupture of membranes are common reasons to go to the hospital.
perOption.c: Waiting that long may be too late.
perOption.d: This is not a sign of labor; decreased fetal movement would need reporting.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach when to come in during labor.

questions.stem: At a 9-month well-baby visit, the parent says the infant is a fussy eater and spits up often. The nurse reviews the weight-for-age growth chart. Highlight the findings that need follow-up.

rationale.correct: Crossing two or more major percentile lines downward suggests growth faltering and needs evaluation of feeding and health.

perOption.r3: A drop across major percentile lines needs attention.
perOption.r4: Continued decline suggests failure to thrive.
perOption.r5: Falling across several percentile lines needs evaluation.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)

questions.stem: A client with bipolar disorder has stopped speaking, stares for long periods, holds odd postures for hours and resists being moved. The client has eaten and drunk almost nothing for 2 days. Temperature is 37.4 °C (99.3 °F), heart rate 102/min, and the client takes no antipsychotics. Complete the diagram by placing the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

actions.text: Prepare to give lorazepam as prescribed
Monitor intake and arrange fluids and nutrition
Force the client's limbs into a normal position
Leave the client alone so the client is not overstimulated
Give an antipsychotic at a high dose

parameters.text: Fluid intake, urine output and vital signs
Ability to move, speak and eat
Body weight measured once a week
Pupil size and reaction to light
Bowel sounds in each of the four quadrants

rationale.correct: Catatonia is treated with benzodiazepines and sometimes ECT; prevent dehydration, malnutrition, pressure injury and clots, and avoid antipsychotics until assessed.

perOption.c1: Mutism, staring, posturing and resistance to movement with poor intake are catatonia.
perOption.c2: NMS follows antipsychotics and causes high fever and rigidity; the client takes none.
perOption.c3: Posturing and resistance to movement point to catatonia.
perOption.a1: Benzodiazepines are first-line and often work quickly.
perOption.a2: Poor intake can lead to dehydration and malnutrition.
perOption.a4: The client needs close monitoring and care.
perOption.a5: Antipsychotics can worsen catatonia or trigger NMS.
perOption.p1: Dehydration and autonomic changes are risks.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with terminal cancer asks the nurse, "Am I dying?" What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "Don't think about that. Let's focus on getting you comfortable."
"What have you noticed that makes you ask me that today?"
"Your doctor is the one who can answer questions like that."
"Everyone dies someday, so try not to worry about it."

rationale.correct: When a client asks about dying, explore what they know and feel before giving information, and involve the team.

perOption.b: An open response lets the client share fears and what they already know.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to a client asking about death.

questions.stem: A nurse educator uses four short descriptions of clients and students to teach staff how anxiety affects attention and behavior. For each description, indicate the level of anxiety.

rows.text: A student feels alert and focused before an exam and learns well
A client focuses on one worry, misses some details but can follow directions
A client cannot focus on anything but the fear and needs direction for simple tasks
A client is screaming, running and cannot follow any instructions

rationale.correct: Anxiety levels: mild (alert, learning improves), moderate (narrowed focus), severe (very narrow, needs direction) and panic (disorganized, unsafe).

perOption.r2:c2: Narrowed attention with ability to follow directions is moderate.
perOption.r2:c3: The client can still follow directions.
perOption.r3:c3: Very narrow focus needing direction is severe anxiety.
perOption.r3:c4: The client can still respond to direction.
perOption.r4:c4: Disorganized behavior and inability to function is panic.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: Which behaviors suggest a client's agitation is escalating toward aggression? Select all that apply.

options.text: Pacing faster and faster
Clenching fists and jaw
Speaking louder and using threats
Sitting quietly and reading
Staring at staff and moving into their personal space
Asking politely for a snack

rationale.correct: Signs of escalating aggression: pacing, muscle tension, loud speech, threats, staring and invading personal space.

perOption.a: Increasing motor activity is an early sign.
perOption.e: Invading space is a warning sign.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with anorexia nervosa is in an inpatient refeeding program. Which outcome is the most appropriate weekly goal?

options.text: A weight gain of about 0.5 to 1 kg (1 to 2 lb) per week
A weight gain of 4 kg (9 lb) per week to restore weight quickly
Stable weight with no gain, so the client feels in control
Choosing meals without staff input or supervision

rationale.correct: In anorexia, aim for gradual weight gain of about 0.5 to 1 kg per week inpatient, with supervised meals and monitoring for refeeding syndrome.

perOption.a: Gradual gain lowers the risk of refeeding syndrome.
perOption.b: Rapid gain increases the risk of refeeding syndrome.
perOption.c: Weight restoration is a treatment goal.
perOption.d: Meals are supervised early in treatment.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client is starting nicotine patches to quit smoking. Which statement shows correct understanding?

options.text: "I can keep smoking a few cigarettes a day while I wear the patch."
"I'll put on a new patch each day on a different hairless spot."
"I'll cut the patch in half when I want a smaller dose."
"I'll stop the patch suddenly once I've gone a week without cigarettes."

rationale.correct: Nicotine patches: apply a new patch daily to a rotated site, do not smoke while wearing it and taper over weeks.

perOption.a: Smoking while wearing the patch can cause nicotine toxicity.
perOption.b: Daily patches on rotated sites reduce skin irritation.
perOption.c: Patches are not cut; lower-dose patches are used to taper.
perOption.d: The dose is tapered over weeks.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A psychiatric unit is training staff to recognize when to step in with an agitated client before violence occurs. Place the phases of the assault cycle in order.

items.text: Recovery: the client begins to calm down
Triggering: a stressor starts the client's response
Crisis: the client may become physically aggressive
Escalation: the client becomes more agitated and loses control
Post-crisis depression: the client may feel remorse or exhaustion

rationale.correct: Assault cycle: triggering, escalation, crisis, recovery and post-crisis depression; intervene early in triggering and escalation.

perOption.a: The event that starts the cycle.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: An older client from a culture where families make health decisions together is told about a serious diagnosis. The client's son asks the team to discuss treatment only with the family. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Tell the son that the law requires the client to make each decision alone
Ask the client privately how they want information shared
Agree with the son and give the information to the family from now on
Refer the family to the ethics committee before talking to anyone

rationale.correct: Ask the client directly how they want information shared and whether they want family to take part in decisions.

perOption.a: Clients may choose to involve family; the client's own preference must be asked.
perOption.b: Respecting culture means asking the client's own preference about involving family.
perOption.c: The client must be asked first.
perOption.d: A simple conversation with the client usually resolves this.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
